pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, with reference to their own code; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through `SCOUT_TOP=5 scout scan --top 10`. Which value wins, and how does your code know the user typed the flag at all?
expected_points: precedence is defaults < config file < environment < flags
the flag wins even though 10 is also the default value
cobra's Changed field distinguishes 'typed' from 'sitting at the default'; the same question is answered by pointer fields in the config file and by a non-empty environment value
every source collapses into one Settings struct before any handler works

questions.prompt: Someone presses Ctrl-C while `scout authors` is running. Trace what happens from the signal to the exit code.
expected_points: signal.NotifyContext in main turns SIGINT into a cancelled context instead of killing the process
the context reaches the handler through ExecuteContext and cmd.Context()
exec.CommandContext kills the child — or refuses to start it if the context is already cancelled
ctx.Err() is checked before classifying the failure, because a killed child looks like an ordinary non-zero exit
Execute maps context.Canceled to 130 and prints one line on stderr; stop() restores the default handler so a second Ctrl-C still works

questions.prompt: Your tool exits 2 for a bad flag and 1 for an unreadable directory. Why is that distinction worth the code it costs?
expected_points: exit codes are the contract with scripts and CI: 2 means the invocation is broken and will stay broken, 1 means the work failed and a retry might not
implemented as an ErrUsage sentinel wrapped into parse and validation failures, classified once by exitCode with errors.Is
no handler knows about exit codes and no error carries one around
honest about the gap: cobra's unknown-command error is not classifiable without matching on message text

questions.prompt: Your tests run the whole program without a subprocess, a terminal, or a real environment variable. What makes that possible, and what did you have to give up to get it?
expected_points: App carries Getenv, ConfigDir, Git and StdoutIsTerminal; main is the only code that touches the real ones
handlers write to cmd.OutOrStdout()/cmd.ErrOrStderr() and return errors rather than calling os.Exit
NewRootCmd is a constructor, so each run gets a tree with no leftover flag state
the cost is a little plumbing: values that could have been read anywhere now have to be passed in — and that is exactly what makes them substitutable

questions.prompt: You are cutting v1.0.0 of scout. How does the tag end up inside the binary, and what does `--version` print for a build made from a dirty working tree?
expected_points: go build -ldflags "-X main.version=… -X main.commit=… -X main.date=…" patches package-level string vars at link time (consts cannot be patched)
an unpatched build honestly reports the defaults dev/none/unknown rather than faking a version
cross-compilation is GOOS/GOARCH with CGO_ENABLED=0; the same source produces every artifact
the version report is one struct so text and --json say the same thing

questions.prompt: Which parts of scout's output are you allowed to change in a patch release, and which are not?
expected_points: the human table is presentation: columns, colour and wording can change
the JSON documents are an API other people's scripts parse and change like one
documents rather than bare arrays so fields can be added; empty slices encode as [] not null; never any escape sequences in JSON
flag names and exit codes are also published interface

questions.prompt: The tests make the test binary re-execute itself as a fake `git`. Why not just require git to be installed, or commit a small fixture binary?
expected_points: determinism: canned output, canned exit code, canned stderr, identical everywhere
no external dependency, no network, no build step, works on every platform the tests run on

the sentinel environment variable is inherited by the child; the helper does nothing during an ordinary run and ends with os.Exit so the testing framework's own output never pollutes the parent's stdout
